name: Oswald Efficiency Factor (Estimate)
description: Provides an empirical estimate of the Oswald span efficiency factor from wing aspect ratio. It uses the fitted expression 1.78 times one minus 0.045 times aspect ratio to the 0.68 power minus 0.64, capturing how induced-drag efficiency varies with planform.
notes: This is an empirical correlation for straight, moderate-aspect-ratio wings and is not exact. The factor is dimensionless and typically less than one; it feeds directly into induced-drag estimates.

name: Required Lift Coefficient (Level Flight)
description: Gives the lift coefficient an aircraft needs to sustain level flight. It equals twice the weight divided by air density times airspeed squared times wing area, so the required coefficient falls steeply as speed increases.
notes: Assumes lift exactly balances weight in steady level flight. Because speed is squared, the required lift coefficient drops sharply at higher airspeeds; use consistent SI units.

name: Induced Drag Coefficient
description: Computes the lift-induced drag coefficient of a wing. It equals the lift coefficient squared divided by pi times the aspect ratio times the Oswald efficiency, showing that induced drag grows with the square of lift and shrinks for high-aspect-ratio wings.
notes: Covers only induced (lift-dependent) drag; add zero-lift drag for total drag. Higher aspect ratio and higher Oswald efficiency both reduce this component.

name: Maximum Lift-to-Drag Ratio
description: Estimates the maximum lift-to-drag ratio achievable by an aircraft. It equals half the square root of pi times aspect ratio times Oswald efficiency divided by the zero-lift drag coefficient, a key measure of aerodynamic efficiency.
notes: This gives the peak L/D for a parabolic drag polar, occurring at a specific lift coefficient. High aspect ratio, high Oswald efficiency, and low zero-lift drag all raise it.

name: Wing Loading
description: Gives the wing loading of an aircraft, the weight carried per unit wing area. It equals the weight divided by the wing area, a basic parameter influencing stall speed, maneuverability, and ride quality.
notes: Here weight is a force in newtons, so the result is in N/m^2, not the mass-based kg/m^2 sometimes quoted. Higher wing loading generally raises stall and cruise speeds.

name: Stall Speed
description: Computes the minimum airspeed at which a wing can support the aircraft weight. It equals the square root of twice the weight divided by air density times wing area times the maximum lift coefficient, marking the onset of stall.
notes: Uses the maximum lift coefficient, so it gives the lowest flyable speed for the given configuration. Stall speed rises with weight and falls in denser air; use consistent SI units.

name: Blasius Skin Friction Coefficient
description: Gives the average skin friction coefficient for laminar flow over a flat plate from the Blasius solution. It equals 1.328 divided by the square root of the Reynolds number, decreasing as the Reynolds number rises.
notes: Valid only for laminar boundary layers on a flat plate; it does not apply once the flow transitions to turbulence. Reynolds number is based on the plate length.

name: Prandtl-Glauert Compressibility Correction
description: Applies the Prandtl-Glauert rule to correct an incompressible pressure coefficient for compressibility. It equals the incompressible pressure coefficient divided by the square root of one minus the Mach number squared, amplifying the coefficient as speed approaches sonic.
notes: Valid only in subsonic flow well below Mach 1; it diverges at Mach 1 and fails in transonic and supersonic regimes. It is a linearized, small-disturbance approximation.

name: Isentropic Stagnation Temperature
description: Computes the stagnation (total) temperature of a compressible flow brought isentropically to rest. It equals the static temperature times one plus the quantity gamma minus one over two times the Mach number squared, rising with Mach number.
notes: Assumes isentropic flow of a perfect gas and temperatures in absolute units (kelvin). The stagnation temperature is always at or above the static temperature.

name: Isentropic Stagnation Pressure Ratio
description: Gives the ratio of stagnation to static pressure for isentropic compressible flow. It equals one plus the quantity gamma minus one over two times the Mach number squared, raised to gamma over gamma minus one, growing steeply with Mach number.
notes: Assumes isentropic flow of a perfect gas. The result is the total-to-static pressure ratio; multiply by static pressure to get stagnation pressure.

name: Mach Angle
description: Gives the Mach angle of the shock cone formed by a body in supersonic flight. It equals the arcsine of one divided by the Mach number, so the cone narrows as the Mach number increases.
notes: Defined only for supersonic flow where the Mach number exceeds one; the result is in radians. Higher Mach numbers produce a smaller, more swept-back Mach cone.

name: Adiabatic Recovery Temperature
description: Estimates the wall temperature reached by an insulated surface in high-speed flow. It equals the static temperature times one plus the recovery factor times gamma minus one over two times the Mach number squared, accounting for incomplete stagnation heating.
notes: The recovery factor (below one) reduces heating relative to full stagnation; it is roughly the square root of the Prandtl number for laminar flow. Use absolute temperatures.

name: Normal Shock Downstream Mach Number
description: Computes the Mach number behind a normal shock from the upstream Mach number. It follows the Rankine-Hugoniot relation using the specific heat ratio, always yielding a subsonic value downstream of the shock.
notes: Valid for a stationary normal shock with upstream Mach number greater than one; the downstream flow is always subsonic. Assumes a perfect gas with constant gamma.

name: Normal Shock Static Pressure Ratio
description: Gives the static pressure jump across a normal shock. It equals one plus two gamma over gamma plus one times the upstream Mach number squared minus one, so pressure rises sharply as the upstream Mach number grows.
notes: Valid for a stationary normal shock with upstream Mach number above one; the ratio is always greater than one. Assumes a perfect gas with constant gamma.

name: Normal Shock Density Ratio
description: Gives the density jump across a normal shock. It equals gamma plus one times the upstream Mach number squared divided by gamma minus one times the upstream Mach number squared plus two, approaching a finite limit at high Mach numbers.
notes: Valid for a stationary normal shock with upstream Mach above one. Unlike pressure, the density ratio saturates to a maximum of (gamma+1)/(gamma-1) as Mach number grows large.

name: Prandtl-Meyer Function
description: Computes the Prandtl-Meyer angle describing how much a supersonic flow can turn through an isentropic expansion. It combines two arctangent terms with the specific heat ratio and Mach number, increasing with Mach number.
notes: Defined only for supersonic flow (Mach number above one); the result is in radians. It measures the turning angle from Mach 1, used to analyze expansion fans.

name: True Airspeed from Density Ratio
description: Converts calibrated airspeed to true airspeed by multiplying by the square root of the sea-level to actual air density ratio. As air thins with altitude, true airspeed exceeds the calibrated (indicated) value.
notes: This simplified relation ignores compressibility and instrument or position error, so it is most accurate at low speeds and moderate altitude. Densities must share the same unit.

name: True Airspeed from Mach Number
description: Computes true airspeed as the Mach number times the local speed of sound, where the speed of sound is the square root of the specific heat ratio times the specific gas constant times the static temperature. Higher temperature raises the speed of sound and thus true airspeed.
notes: Temperature must be absolute (kelvin), not Celsius, and is the static air temperature at altitude. The variable labeled g here is the specific heat ratio (about 1.4 for air), not gravity.

name: Density Altitude (Approx)
description: Estimates density altitude by adding to the pressure altitude a correction of about 118.8 feet per degree Celsius that the outside air temperature exceeds the standard temperature at that pressure altitude. It gives the altitude the air density corresponds to in a standard atmosphere.
notes: The 15-0.00198*PA term is the ISA standard temperature in Celsius at that pressure altitude. Inputs are in feet and Celsius; this is a linear approximation to the exact density-altitude relation.

name: Pressure Altitude (Approx)
description: Estimates pressure altitude by adjusting the field elevation for the difference between the standard sea-level pressure of 1013.25 hPa and the current altimeter setting, at about 30 feet per hectopascal. It gives the altitude in the standard atmosphere matching the ambient pressure.
notes: Below standard pressure (QNH), the correction adds height; above it, it subtracts. Inputs use feet and hPa; the 30 ft per hPa factor is a near-surface approximation.

name: Rate of Climb (Excess Power)
description: Computes the maximum rate of climb from the excess thrust over drag times airspeed, divided by weight. It expresses how fast an aircraft can gain altitude using the specific excess power available.
notes: Assumes a small climb angle so thrust and drag act along the flight path; forces are in newtons and the result is in m/s. It gives the instantaneous, steady rate at that speed.

name: Climb Gradient Angle
description: Computes the steady climb angle as the arcsine of the excess thrust over drag divided by weight. It gives the flight path angle an aircraft can sustain in a straight climb at that thrust setting.
notes: Requires thrust above drag and the ratio at most 1, or the arcsine is undefined. Forces in newtons; the result is in radians. Assumes steady, unaccelerated climb.

name: Turn Radius
description: Computes the radius of a level, coordinated turn from the true airspeed, gravity, and load factor. A higher load factor (steeper bank) tightens the turn, while higher speed widens it.
notes: Requires a load factor above 1; at n=1 the turn radius is infinite (wings level). Assumes a coordinated level turn. Airspeed in m/s gives radius in meters.

name: Turn Rate
description: Computes the angular turn rate of a level, coordinated turn from gravity, load factor, and true airspeed. A higher load factor speeds the turn while higher airspeed slows it.
notes: Requires a load factor above 1; at n=1 the turn rate is zero. Assumes a coordinated level turn. Result is in radians per second with airspeed in m/s.

name: Load Factor from Bank Angle
description: Computes the load factor in a level, coordinated turn as one over the cosine of the bank angle. It gives the multiple of normal weight the wings must support to hold altitude at that bank.
notes: Bank angle is in radians and must stay below 90 degrees, where the load factor grows without bound. Valid only for a level, coordinated turn with no climb or descent.

name: Stall Speed in Turn
description: Computes the stall speed in a turn as the level-flight stall speed times the square root of the load factor. The increased load in a banked turn raises the speed at which the wing stalls.
notes: The load factor is dimensionless (n=1/cos(bank) for a level turn), and stall speed scales with its square root. Result shares the unit of the input stall speed.

name: Standard Rate Turn Bank Angle
description: Computes the bank angle required for a given turn rate at a given true airspeed, as the arctangent of the turn rate times airspeed divided by gravity. Faster aircraft need a steeper bank to hold the same turn rate.
notes: Turn rate is in radians per second (a standard-rate turn is 3 deg/s, about 0.0524 rad/s) and airspeed in m/s. The result is in radians and assumes a coordinated level turn.

name: Crosswind Component
description: Computes the crosswind component as the wind speed times the sine of the angle between the wind and the runway heading. It gives the part of the wind acting across the runway, which matters for takeoff and landing limits.
notes: The angle is in radians, measured between the wind direction and the runway. At 90 degrees the full wind is crosswind; the complementary cosine term gives the headwind component.

name: Headwind Component
description: Computes the component of the wind blowing straight down the runway by projecting the wind vector onto the runway heading, V times cos(theta). A positive result is a headwind that shortens takeoff and landing rolls; a negative result is a tailwind.
notes: theta is the angle between the wind and the runway centerline in radians (0 = pure headwind). At theta = pi/2 the headwind is zero, and beyond that the value turns negative, indicating a tailwind.

name: Ground Speed (Wind Triangle)
description: Solves the wind triangle for ground speed using the law of cosines, combining true airspeed and wind speed separated by the angle between the wind and the desired track. The result is the actual speed over the ground.
notes: theta is the angle between the wind vector and the intended track in radians. This gives magnitude only; the required heading (wind correction angle) must be found separately.

name: Wind Correction Angle
description: Gives the angle the aircraft must crab into the wind to hold the desired track, from asin(Ws*sin(wa)/TAS). It balances the crosswind component against true airspeed so the ground track stays on course.
notes: wa is the angle between the wind and the desired track in radians. The formula requires Ws*sin(wa) to be no larger than TAS; otherwise the crosswind exceeds airspeed and no valid correction exists.

name: Glide Distance
description: Estimates the horizontal distance an unpowered aircraft can glide from a given altitude by multiplying the height by the glide ratio, h times LD. A glide ratio of 17 means 17 meters forward per meter of descent.
notes: Assumes a steady glide at the best lift-to-drag ratio in still air, ignoring wind. Head or tail winds shorten or extend the actual reach.

name: Best Glide Speed
description: Gives the airspeed for maximum lift-to-drag ratio, where glide range is greatest, from the wing loading and the drag polar coefficients. It is the speed that minimizes the glide angle in unpowered flight.
notes: Uses a parabolic drag polar Cd = Cd0 + K*CL^2 and requires consistent SI units (W in newtons, S in square meters). Weight, air density, and configuration all shift this speed.

name: Minimum Sink Speed
description: Gives the airspeed that produces the slowest rate of descent (minimum sink), which maximizes time aloft in a glide. It occurs at the maximum of CL^1.5/CD and is lower than the best-glide speed.
notes: Based on a parabolic drag polar; the factor 3 distinguishes it from best-glide speed. Minimum sink maximizes endurance, not range. Use consistent SI units.

name: Breguet Range (Jet)
description: Estimates the maximum still-air range of a jet aircraft in cruise as V/c times the lift-to-drag ratio times the natural log of the initial-to-final weight ratio. Burning more fuel (larger Wi/Wf) or a higher L/D extends range.
notes: Assumes constant speed, L/D, and thrust specific fuel consumption. c is per second, so keep V in m/s; the result is in meters. Wf must be less than Wi.

name: Breguet Endurance (Jet)
description: Estimates how long a jet can stay airborne on a given fuel load as (1/c) times the lift-to-drag ratio times the natural log of the initial-to-final weight ratio. Unlike range, it does not depend on cruise speed.
notes: Assumes constant L/D and thrust specific fuel consumption. With c in per second the result is in seconds; Wf must be less than Wi. Maximum endurance occurs at maximum L/D.

name: Breguet Range (Propeller)
description: Estimates the still-air range of a propeller aircraft as the propeller efficiency divided by brake specific fuel consumption, times L/D, times the natural log of the initial-to-final weight ratio. Higher propeller efficiency and L/D extend range.
notes: Assumes constant efficiency, L/D, and fuel consumption. Here c is per meter (energy-based BSFC form), giving a result in meters; Wf must be less than Wi.

name: Lift Coefficient (from Lift)
description: Back-solves the lift equation for the dimensionless lift coefficient, CL = 2L/(rho*V^2*S). It expresses how much lift the wing generates relative to dynamic pressure and wing area.
notes: V is true airspeed and appears squared, so CL is very sensitive to speed. Use consistent SI units; the result is dimensionless.

name: Power Required (Level Flight)
description: Gives the power needed to overcome drag in steady level flight as drag times airspeed, D times V. This is the power that must be delivered to the airframe to hold speed and altitude.
notes: This is power required to overcome drag, not engine shaft or thrust power; propulsive efficiency losses are not included. Keep D in newtons and V in m/s for a result in watts.

name: Thrust Required (Level Flight)
description: Gives the thrust needed for steady level flight as weight divided by the lift-to-drag ratio, W/LD. In equilibrium lift equals weight and thrust equals drag, so a higher L/D lowers the thrust required.
notes: Valid for unaccelerated level flight where lift equals weight. It equals drag at that condition; climbing or turning raises the required thrust.

name: Chord Reynolds Number
description: Computes the dimensionless Reynolds number based on wing chord, rho*V*ch/mu, comparing inertial to viscous forces in the airflow over the airfoil. It indicates whether the boundary layer tends toward laminar or turbulent flow.
notes: Uses chord length as the characteristic dimension. Keep all inputs in SI units (density in kg/m^3, viscosity in Pa*s); the result is dimensionless.

name: Wing Aspect Ratio
description: Computes the wing aspect ratio as span squared divided by wing area, b^2/S. Higher aspect ratios reduce induced drag and improve gliding efficiency, at the cost of structural weight and roll response.
notes: The b^2/S form works for any planform, not just rectangular wings (for a rectangular wing it reduces to span/chord). The result is dimensionless.

name: Mean Aerodynamic Chord (Tapered Wing)
description: Computes the mean aerodynamic chord of a linearly tapered wing from the root chord and taper ratio. The MAC is the representative chord used for aerodynamic and stability calculations such as locating the center of gravity.
notes: lam is tip chord divided by root chord (0 to 1). Assumes a straight linear taper; at lam = 1 (no taper) the MAC equals the root chord.

name: Takeoff Ground Roll (Approx)
description: Estimates the ground distance to reach liftoff speed under constant acceleration, Vlof^2/(2*acc), from the kinematic relation between speed, acceleration, and distance. It gives the runway length used before the wheels leave the ground.
notes: Assumes a constant mean acceleration and a start from rest. Real rolls vary as thrust and drag change with speed; this is a first-order estimate only.

name: Landing Ground Roll (Approx)
description: Estimates the ground distance to stop from touchdown speed under constant deceleration, Vtd^2/(2*dec), from the kinematic speed-distance relation. It gives the runway length used from touchdown to a full stop.
notes: Assumes a constant mean deceleration to a full stop. Actual braking varies with braking force, aerodynamic drag, and runway condition; this is a first-order estimate.

name: Energy Height (Specific Energy)
description: Computes specific energy (energy height), the total mechanical energy per unit weight expressed as an altitude, h + V^2/(2g). It represents the height the aircraft could reach if all kinetic energy were traded for potential energy.
notes: V is true airspeed. Both terms come out in meters, so the sum is a height, not a literal altitude the aircraft occupies. It ignores drag and thrust during the trade.

name: Load Factor in Pull-up
description: Gives the load factor (g-force) during a level pull-up as 1 + V^2/(g*Rp), the sum of supporting weight plus the centripetal acceleration of the curved path. A tighter radius or higher speed raises the g-load on airframe and crew.
notes: Applies at the bottom of a vertical pull-up where lift supports weight and turns the aircraft. The result is in multiples of g; a value of 1 means unaccelerated flight.

name: Maneuvering (Corner) Speed
description: Gives the corner (maneuvering) speed, the lowest speed at which the wing can reach its maximum load factor before stalling, sqrt(2*nmax*W/(rho*S*CLmax)). It is the speed for the tightest turn without structural overstress.
notes: At this speed full aft stick reaches limit load and stall simultaneously; above it the wing can overstress the airframe, below it the wing stalls first. Use consistent SI units.

name: ISA Temperature (Troposphere)
description: Gives the air temperature at a given altitude in the troposphere under the International Standard Atmosphere, 288.15 - 0.0065*h. It applies the standard sea-level temperature of 288.15 K and a lapse rate of 6.5 K per kilometer.
notes: h is geopotential altitude in meters and the result is in kelvin. Valid only up to the tropopause at about 11000 m, where the temperature stops falling.

name: ISA Pressure (Barometric)
description: Gives the atmospheric pressure at altitude in the troposphere under the International Standard Atmosphere, 101325*(1 - 2.25577e-5*h)^5.25588. It starts from the standard sea-level pressure of 101325 Pa.
notes: h is altitude in meters and the result is in pascals. The exponent embeds the standard lapse rate and gravity, so it is valid only below the tropopause (about 11000 m).

name: ISA Density (Barometric)
description: Gives the air density at altitude in the troposphere under the International Standard Atmosphere, 1.225*(1 - 2.25577e-5*h)^4.25588. It starts from the standard sea-level density of 1.225 kg/m^3.
notes: h is altitude in meters and the result is in kg/m^3. The exponent differs from the pressure formula by one because density also depends on temperature; valid below about 11000 m.

name: Propeller Advance Ratio
description: Computes the propeller advance ratio, the dimensionless ratio of forward airspeed to the product of rotation rate and diameter, V/(nr*D). It characterizes the propeller operating point, analogous to the angle of attack of the blades.
notes: nr is rotations per second (not radians per second or RPM), and D is the full diameter. The result is dimensionless; propeller efficiency curves are plotted against it.

name: Propeller Tip Mach Number
description: Gives the Mach number at the propeller blade tip by combining the forward airspeed with the tip rotational speed vectorially and dividing by the local speed of sound, sqrt(V^2 + (pi*nr*D)^2)/a. It flags when tips approach compressibility limits.
notes: pi*nr*D is the tip rotational speed for rotation rate nr in rev/s and diameter D. Tip Mach numbers approaching 1 cause efficiency loss and noise; keep well below unity.

name: Specific Fuel Consumption
description: Computes specific fuel consumption as the fuel flow rate divided by the thrust or power produced, a standard measure of propulsion efficiency used to compare engines.
notes: Use thrust (giving TSFC, thrust-specific fuel consumption) for jet and turbofan engines, or shaft power (giving PSFC) for turboprop and piston engines; keep the output unit consistent with the quantity chosen. Lower values indicate a more fuel-efficient engine.

name: Rate of Descent (Glide)
description: Estimates the steady-state rate of descent during a power-off glide from the true airspeed TAS and the lift-to-drag ratio LD, using the standard aviation approximation ROD = TAS × 101.3 / (L/D).
notes: The constant 101.3 converts knots to feet per minute (1 kt ≈ 101.3 ft/min) under the small-angle assumption that sink rate equals horizontal speed divided by L/D. A higher L/D or lower airspeed gives a shallower descent.

name: Haversine Great-Circle Distance
description: Computes the great-circle distance between two points on a sphere from their latitudes and longitudes using the haversine formula, returning the shortest surface distance for Earth radius R. It is the standard method for distances between geographic coordinates.
notes: Latitudes and longitudes are entered in degrees and converted internally to radians. It models Earth as a perfect sphere, so results carry a small error versus the true ellipsoidal shape; distance shares the units of R.

name: Initial Great-Circle Bearing
description: Computes the initial compass course, in degrees, to steer from point 1 (lat1, lon1) toward point 2 (lat2, lon2) along the shortest great-circle path over a spherical Earth. It gives the forward azimuth at the departure point.
notes: Coordinates are in degrees; the formula converts internally. The atan result lies in -90 to +90, so add 360 or resolve the quadrant to get a true 0-360 bearing. The bearing continuously changes along a great circle.

name: Equirectangular Approximation Distance
description: Estimates the distance between two points on Earth by treating a small patch of the sphere as a flat rectangle, scaling east-west spacing by the cosine of the mean latitude. It is faster but less exact than the haversine formula.
notes: Coordinates are in degrees and R sets the output unit (km here). Accuracy degrades over long distances and near the poles; best for short, local spans where a flat-Earth approximation is acceptable.

name: Length of One Degree of Latitude
description: Gives the ground distance in meters spanned by one degree of latitude at latitude phi on the WGS84 ellipsoid. The value grows slightly from equator toward the poles because the meridian curvature changes.
notes: Latitude phi is in degrees. This is a series fit to the ellipsoid, so it already accounts for Earth's flattening; do not use a fixed 111 km value if precision matters.

name: Length of One Degree of Longitude
description: Gives the ground distance in meters spanned by one degree of longitude at latitude phi on the WGS84 ellipsoid. The value shrinks from about 111 km at the equator toward zero at the poles as meridians converge.
notes: Latitude phi is in degrees. Distance depends strongly on latitude via the cosine term; at high latitudes a degree of longitude is much shorter than a degree of latitude.

name: Cross-Track Distance (Great Circle)
description: Finds the perpendicular distance a third point lies off a great-circle track, given its distance and bearing from the track start (d13, brng13) and the track bearing (brng12). The sign indicates which side of the track the point is on.
notes: Distances and R share the same unit (km); bearings are in degrees. d13/R is a central angle in radians, so R must match the units of d13. A small d13/R keeps the approximation valid.

name: Along-Track Distance (Great Circle)
description: Computes how far along a great-circle track the closest point to a third point lies, measured from the track start, using the start-to-point distance d13 and the cross-track distance dxt. It complements the cross-track distance.
notes: All distances and R use the same unit (km). d13 and dxt must come from the same reference geometry; the acos argument should stay within -1 to 1, which holds when dxt does not exceed d13.

name: Dead Reckoning New Latitude
description: Estimates the new latitude after running distance d on course brng from a starting latitude lat1, using dead reckoning on a sphere. Only the northward component of travel (cosine of the course) shifts latitude.
notes: d and R share a unit (km); the result is in degrees. This assumes a straight rhumb-like short run and ignores the longitude change; valid for short distances where curvature is small.

name: Dead Reckoning New Longitude
description: Estimates the new longitude after running distance d on course brng from a start point, dividing the east-west travel by the cosine of the starting latitude to convert departure into a longitude change.
notes: d and R share a unit (km); the result is in degrees. Uses the starting latitude for the cosine, so it degrades over long runs; the cosine term makes longitude changes large near the poles.

name: Drift Angle from Current
description: Computes the drift (set) angle in degrees that a boat must offset for, given a cross current of speed vc meeting the heading at a given angle while the boat moves at speed vb. It comes from the sine rule of the velocity triangle.
notes: Speeds vc and vb use the same unit (knots); the angle is in degrees. The current speed must not exceed the boat speed component or the asin argument leaves -1 to 1; the result is the heading correction, not the ground course.

name: Radar Horizon Distance
description: Estimates the radar horizon distance in kilometers for an antenna of height h in meters, using the standard 4.12 sqrt(h) rule that accounts for atmospheric refraction bending radar waves slightly beyond the geometric horizon.
notes: Height h is in meters and the result is in km. The constant 4.12 already includes the standard 4/3 Earth-radius refraction model; abnormal atmospheric conditions (ducting) can extend the range considerably.

name: Dip of the Sea Horizon
description: Gives the dip of the sea horizon in arcminutes for an observer whose eye is h meters above sea level. Dip is the angle by which the visible horizon lies below the true horizontal and is subtracted when correcting a sextant altitude.
notes: Height of eye h is in meters; the result is in arcminutes. The 1.76 constant includes standard atmospheric refraction; always subtract dip from the sextant altitude during sight reduction.

name: Estimated Time of Arrival
description: Computes the travel time in hours to cover a distance dist at a constant speed over ground, simply distance divided by speed. It gives the estimated time en route for planning an arrival.
notes: Distance is in nautical miles and speed in knots, which are consistent so the result is in hours. Assumes constant speed; convert the decimal hours to hours and minutes for a clock ETA.

name: Rhumb Line Distance (Mercator)
description: Computes the distance along a rhumb line (constant-bearing loxodrome) between two points on a sphere using Mercator projection stretching. A rhumb line is longer than a great circle but keeps a single steady compass course.
notes: Coordinates are in degrees; R sets the unit (km). The stretched-latitude term becomes singular for a due east-west track (lat1 equals lat2), which needs the limiting cosine form instead.

name: Rhumb Line Bearing (Mercator)
description: Computes the constant compass bearing in degrees of the rhumb line joining two points, using the ratio of longitude difference to the difference of Mercator stretched latitudes. This single course is held for the whole passage.
notes: Coordinates are in degrees. The atan output is -90 to +90, so resolve the quadrant from the signs of the longitude and latitude differences to obtain a full 0-360 bearing.

name: Convergence of Meridians
description: Estimates the convergence angle in degrees between two meridians at a given latitude, equal to the longitude difference times the sine of latitude. It is the angular difference between grid north and true north on a map.
notes: The longitude difference is in degrees and the result is in degrees. This is a spherical approximation valid for small longitude spans; convergence grows toward the poles and vanishes at the equator.

name: Clairaut Great-Circle Vertex Latitude
description: Gives the highest latitude reached by a great circle (its vertex) in degrees, from the initial course brng and the latitude lat at a known point, via Clairaut's relation that sin(course) times cos(latitude) stays constant.
notes: Course and latitude are in degrees; the result is the absolute vertex latitude for both hemispheres. The abs makes the answer a magnitude; the actual vertex lies north or south depending on the sailing direction.

name: Distance off by Vertical Sextant Angle
description: Estimates the horizontal distance to an object of known height H by dividing that height by the tangent of the measured vertical angle at the observer. It is a classic way to fix distance off a lighthouse or peak.
notes: Height H is in meters and the result is in meters; the angle is in degrees. Accuracy assumes the object base is at sea level and ignores dip and refraction; small angles give large, sensitive distances.

name: Length of a Nautical Mile at Latitude
description: Gives the length in meters of one nautical mile (one minute of arc of latitude) at latitude phi. Because Earth is an ellipsoid, this varies slightly with latitude around the standard 1852 m value.
notes: Latitude phi is in degrees; the result is in meters. The variation is only a few meters between equator and pole; the international standard nautical mile is fixed at exactly 1852 m regardless of latitude.

name: Groundspeed with Headwind Component
description: Computes groundspeed by subtracting the along-track wind component from true airspeed, where the component is the wind speed times the cosine of the angle between the wind and the aircraft heading.
notes: Speeds share a unit (knots); the wind angle is in degrees. A tailwind (angle near 180) makes the cosine negative and raises groundspeed; this simplified model ignores the crosswind drift component.

name: Departure (Mid-Latitude Sailing)
description: Converts a difference of longitude in minutes into departure (east-west distance) in nautical miles by multiplying by the cosine of the mid latitude, as used in mid-latitude sailing calculations.
notes: The longitude difference is in minutes of arc and the mid latitude in degrees; the result is in nautical miles. Using the mid latitude is an approximation that works best for short north-south spans.

name: Mercator Meridional Parts
description: Computes the meridional parts for latitude phi, the stretched north-south distance in minutes on a Mercator chart measured from the equator. Meridional parts let rhumb-line problems be solved with plane trigonometry.
notes: Latitude phi is in degrees; the result is in minutes of longitude on the projection. This spherical form omits the small ellipsoidal correction used on precise nautical charts.

name: Amplitude of a Celestial Body
description: Computes the amplitude, the angle in degrees north or south of due east or west at which a celestial body rises or sets, from its declination and the observer latitude. It is used to check compass error at sunrise or sunset.
notes: Declination and latitude are in degrees. Valid only where the argument of asin stays within -1 to 1, which fails when the declination magnitude exceeds the co-latitude (the body then never sets).

name: Latitude by Meridian Altitude
description: Determines the observer latitude in degrees from the observed meridian altitude of a body and its declination, using the meridian passage relation latitude equals 90 minus altitude plus declination. It is the classic noon-sight latitude.
notes: Altitude and declination are in degrees. This particular sign form assumes the body bears south with its zenith distance measured to the north; declination and the zenith-distance sense must match the observation geometry.

name: True Heading from Compass Heading
description: Converts a compass heading to true heading by applying magnetic variation and compass deviation, TH = CH + variation + deviation, the standard compass-correction chain used in marine and air navigation.
notes: Enter variation and deviation as signed values (east positive, west negative, by convention). If the true heading falls outside 0-360, add or subtract 360 as needed.

name: Velocity Made Good
description: Computes velocity made good, VMG = speed*cos(angle), the component of a vessel's speed directed toward a target course or upwind/downwind mark, from its actual speed and the angle between its heading and that direction.
notes: The angle is entered in degrees and converted internally to radians. VMG is at its maximum (equal to speed) when angle is 0 and drops to zero at 90 degrees off course.

name: Engine Power from Torque (SI)
description: Computes mechanical power in watts from torque and rotational speed, as torque times angular velocity 2π·rpm/60. It converts engine speed in rpm to radians per second before multiplying by torque.
notes: Torque must be in newton-metres and speed in rpm for a watt result. Divide by 1000 for kilowatts or by 745.7 for horsepower.

name: Engine Horsepower from Torque and RPM
description: Gives engine power in horsepower from torque in pound-feet and engine speed, as torque times rpm divided by 5252. The constant 5252 arises from unit conversion and the point where torque and horsepower curves cross.
notes: Torque must be in lb·ft and speed in rpm for the 5252 constant to give mechanical (imperial) horsepower. This is a fixed-unit shortcut, not the SI form.

name: Engine Torque from Power (SI, RPM)
description: Solves for torque in newton-metres from power and engine speed, as P·60/(2π·rpm). It is the inverse of the SI power formula, converting rpm to angular velocity before dividing power by it.
notes: Power must be in watts and speed in rpm to get newton-metres. Torque falls as engine speed rises for a fixed power output.

name: Top Speed from Power (Drag-Limited)
description: Estimates the drag-limited top speed as the cube root of 2P/(rho·Cd·A), the speed at which available power equals aerodynamic drag power. Doubling power raises top speed by only about 26 percent.
notes: Uses SI units: power in watts, air density in kg/m³, area in m², giving speed in m/s. It ignores rolling resistance and drivetrain losses, so real top speed is lower.

name: Aerodynamic Drag Force (Vehicle)
description: Computes aerodynamic drag force from air density, drag coefficient, frontal area, and speed, as 0.5·rho·Cd·A·v². Drag rises with the square of speed, so it dominates resistance at high velocity.
notes: Uses SI units throughout, giving force in newtons; speed must be relative to the air, so headwinds add to it. Drag coefficient and frontal area are treated as constant with speed.

name: Aerodynamic Drag Power
description: Gives the power needed to overcome aerodynamic drag at a steady speed, as 0.5·rho·Cd·A·v³. Because it scales with the cube of speed, the power demand climbs steeply as the vehicle goes faster.
notes: SI units give power in watts; v is speed relative to the air. This is only the drag component and excludes rolling resistance, grade, and drivetrain losses.

name: Aerodynamic Downforce
description: Computes aerodynamic downforce from air density, lift coefficient, reference area, and speed, as 0.5·rho·Cl·A·v². It uses the same form as lift, with a downward-directed coefficient to increase tyre grip.
notes: SI units give force in newtons; the coefficient Cl here represents downforce magnitude. Force rises with the square of speed, so downforce is small at low speeds.

name: Wheel Speed from RPM and Tire Radius
description: Converts wheel rotational speed and tyre rolling radius to linear (ground) speed, as 2π·rpm·r/60. It multiplies the wheel's angular velocity in radians per second by the rolling radius.
notes: Rolling radius must be in metres and speed in rpm to get metres per second. Rolling radius is slightly less than the unloaded tyre radius; multiply by 3.6 for km/h.

name: Vehicle Speed from Engine RPM and Gearing
description: Computes road speed from engine rpm, tyre rolling radius, and the gear and final-drive ratios, as 2π·r·rpm/(60·gr·fdr). The two reduction ratios divide engine speed down to wheel speed before converting to linear velocity.
notes: Rolling radius in metres and rpm give metres per second. This assumes no tyre slip or clutch slip; multiply by 3.6 for km/h.

name: Braking Distance (Friction-Limited)
description: Estimates the friction-limited braking distance as v²/(2·mu·g), the distance to stop from speed v under maximum tyre grip. Stopping distance grows with the square of speed.
notes: Uses SI units, giving metres; it excludes reaction distance and assumes a level road with constant friction. Real braking varies with tyre, surface, and ABS behaviour.

name: Total Stopping Distance (Reaction + Braking)
description: Adds the reaction distance v·tr, travelled during the driver's reaction time, to the friction-limited braking distance v²/(2·mu·g) to give total stopping distance. It captures both perception delay and actual braking.
notes: SI units give metres; reaction time is in seconds and the road is assumed level with constant friction. The reaction term grows linearly with speed while braking grows with its square.

name: Longitudinal Acceleration from Tractive Force
description: Computes a vehicle's longitudinal acceleration as the net force (tractive force minus resistance) divided by mass. It applies Newton's second law to the driving and opposing forces along the direction of travel.
notes: Uses SI units, giving metres per second squared; the resistance term should sum aerodynamic, rolling, and grade forces. It ignores rotational inertia of wheels and drivetrain.

name: 0-100 km/h Time (Power-Limited Approx)
description: Estimates the time to accelerate to a target speed under constant power, as kinetic energy m·v²/2 divided by average power P. It equates the energy gained to power multiplied by time.
notes: SI units give seconds; the target speed of 27.78 m/s corresponds to 100 km/h. This idealised model ignores traction limits, drag, and rolling resistance, so it underestimates real times.

name: Vehicle Power-to-Weight Ratio
description: Computes the power-to-weight ratio as power divided by vehicle mass, a key indicator of acceleration potential. Higher values generally mean stronger performance for a given mass.
notes: With power in watts and mass in kilograms the result is watts per kilogram; divide by 1000 for kW/kg. It uses mass, not weight (force), despite the common name.

name: Gradient (Hill-Climbing) Resistance Force
description: Computes the gravity component opposing a vehicle on a slope, as m·g·sin(theta). This grade resistance is the force needed just to hold or climb the incline, separate from rolling and air resistance.
notes: The slope angle theta must be in radians for the sine function. Use the true angle, not percent grade; for small angles sin(theta) is close to the grade fraction.

name: Grade Resistance (Percent Grade)
description: Approximates the grade resistance force from a percent grade, as m·g·p/100. Dividing the percent grade by 100 gives the slope fraction, which for small angles approximates sin(theta).
notes: Grade p is entered as a percentage (for example 8 for an 8 percent grade). This linear approximation slightly overstates resistance on steep grades where sin and tan diverge.

name: Engine Displacement (Bore-Stroke)
description: Computes total engine displacement from bore, stroke, and cylinder count, as (pi/4)·bore²·stroke·n. The pi/4·bore² term is the piston area, multiplied by stroke for one cylinder's swept volume and by the number of cylinders.
notes: Bore and stroke are in centimetres, giving displacement in cubic centimetres; divide by 1000 for litres. This is swept volume only and excludes combustion-chamber (clearance) volume.

name: Mean Piston Speed
description: Calculates the mean piston speed as 2·stroke·rpm/60, the average speed of the piston over a full cycle. Each revolution moves the piston through twice the stroke, and dividing by 60 converts rpm to per-second.
notes: Stroke must be in metres and speed in rpm to give metres per second. High mean piston speeds indicate greater mechanical stress and are a limiting factor in engine design.

name: Otto Cycle Thermal Efficiency
description: Computes the ideal thermal efficiency of the Otto (spark-ignition) cycle as 1 − 1/CR^(k−1), depending only on the compression ratio and the heat capacity ratio. Higher compression ratios yield higher ideal efficiency.
notes: Result is a fraction between 0 and 1; multiply by 100 for percent. This is an air-standard idealisation and overstates real efficiency, which is limited by friction, heat loss, and knock.

name: Brake Specific Fuel Consumption (g/kWh)
description: Computes brake specific fuel consumption in grams per kilowatt-hour from the fuel mass flow rate and brake power. It expresses how much fuel mass an engine burns per unit of useful output energy.
notes: Fuel flow is in kg/s and power in watts; the constant 3.6e9 converts kg/s per watt into g/kWh. Lower BSFC means better fuel efficiency.

name: Fuel Consumption (L/100km)
description: Computes fuel consumption in litres per 100 kilometres from the fuel used and the distance driven, as Vf/d·100. It is the standard European measure where lower values mean better economy.
notes: Fuel is in litres and distance in kilometres. Note this is inversely related to miles-per-gallon style measures: a smaller number is more efficient.

name: Lambda (Air-Fuel Equivalence Ratio)
description: Computes the lambda value as the actual air-fuel ratio divided by the stoichiometric air-fuel ratio. Lambda of 1 is a stoichiometric mixture, above 1 is lean (excess air), and below 1 is rich (excess fuel).
notes: Both ratios are mass-based and dimensionless, so their units cancel. The stoichiometric value depends on the fuel, roughly 14.7 for petrol.

name: Traction-Limited Acceleration
description: Gives the maximum acceleration the tyres can transmit as mu·g, the product of the friction coefficient and gravitational acceleration. It is the grip ceiling regardless of how much engine force is available.
notes: SI units give metres per second squared; this assumes a level surface and weight fully on the driven tyres. Divide by g (9.81) to express the result in units of g-force.

name: Longitudinal Weight Transfer (Braking)
description: Computes the vertical load transferred from the rear axle to the front axle during braking. The transfer force equals vehicle mass times deceleration times the ratio of centre-of-gravity height to wheelbase (h/L)·m·a.
notes: Enter deceleration as a positive value; the result is the load added to the front and removed from the rear. Assumes a rigid vehicle on level ground and ignores aerodynamic and suspension pitch effects.

name: Ackermann Steering Angle
description: Gives the ideal steering angle for a bicycle-model vehicle turning at radius R, as the arctangent of wheelbase L divided by (R − track/2). The result is the wheel angle in radians for geometrically correct low-speed cornering.
notes: This is the angle to the inner wheel path centre; true Ackermann geometry sets slightly different left and right angles. Valid at low speed where tyre slip is negligible; R must exceed half the track width.

name: Turning Radius from Wheelbase and Steer Angle
description: Estimates the turning radius of a vehicle from its wheelbase L divided by the tangent of the steering angle delta. Larger steer angles give tighter (smaller) radii under the low-speed bicycle model.
notes: The steering angle is in radians. Radius grows toward infinity as delta approaches zero, and the model assumes no tyre slip, so it applies to low-speed manoeuvres only.

name: Maximum Cornering Speed (Friction-Limited)
description: Calculates the maximum speed a vehicle can maintain around a corner of radius R before tyres lose grip, as the square root of friction coefficient times gravity times radius. It is the speed at which lateral friction just balances the centripetal demand.
notes: Assumes a flat (unbanked) corner and constant friction coefficient; banking or aerodynamic downforce would allow higher speeds. The friction coefficient is dimensionless and typically below about 1.0 for road tyres.

name: Lateral Load Transfer (Cornering)
description: Estimates the lateral load transferred between the inside and outside wheels during cornering, deltaW = (m*ay*h)/t, from vehicle mass, lateral acceleration, centre-of-gravity height, and track width.
notes: A lower centre of gravity and wider track both reduce load transfer, improving cornering grip balance. Treats the vehicle as a rigid body and ignores suspension roll and weight distribution front-to-rear.

name: Tire Slip Ratio
description: Computes longitudinal tire slip ratio, SR = (v_wheel - v_vehicle)/v_vehicle, comparing the tire's rotational (tread) speed to the vehicle's actual ground speed, as used in traction and ABS control analysis.
notes: Positive values indicate wheelspin (driving), negative values indicate wheel lock-up (braking); both wheel and vehicle speed must use the same unit. Peak longitudinal grip typically occurs around 0.1-0.2 slip ratio.

name: Hull Speed (Displacement Hull)
description: Estimates the traditional hull speed of a displacement boat as 1.34 times the square root of the waterline length in feet, giving the result in knots. It marks the speed where the boat's wave system limits efficient progress.
notes: Waterline length must be entered in feet for the 1.34 coefficient to give knots. This is an empirical rule of thumb, not a hard limit; light or planing hulls can exceed it.

name: Speed-Length Ratio
description: Gives the speed-length ratio, ship speed in knots divided by the square root of waterline length in feet. It is the imperial cousin of the Froude number used to gauge how hard a displacement hull is being driven.
notes: Uses knots and feet by convention; a ratio near 1.34 corresponds to classic hull speed. It is a relative index, not an absolute speed limit.

name: Displacement from Block Coefficient
description: Calculates a vessel's displacement mass by multiplying the block coefficient Cb by the enclosing box volume (length × beam × draft) and the water density. It gives the mass of water the immersed hull displaces.
notes: L, B and T are the waterline length, beam and draft defining the bounding box. Cb (typically 0.4–0.9) is the fraction of that box actually filled by the hull; result is in kilograms with density in kg/m^3.

name: Block Coefficient
description: Computes the block coefficient, the ratio of a hull's displaced volume to the volume of the bounding box formed by length, beam and draft. It is a dimensionless measure of how full or fine the hull form is.
notes: L, B and T must be the waterline dimensions in the same units as the volume. Values run from about 0.4 for fine, fast hulls to over 0.8 for bulky cargo ships.

name: Prismatic Coefficient
description: Gives the prismatic coefficient, the displaced volume divided by the product of the midship section area and the length. It describes how the underwater volume is distributed along the hull's length.
notes: Am is the largest (midship) submerged cross-section, in the same units as volume and length. Low values indicate fine ends; it complements the block coefficient rather than replacing it.

name: Waterplane Area Coefficient
description: Computes the waterplane area coefficient, the actual waterplane area divided by the length times beam rectangle. It indicates how full the hull's outline is at the waterline.
notes: Aw is the horizontal cross-section area at the waterline, in units consistent with L and B. Higher values mean a fuller waterplane, which increases stability and TPC.

name: Admiralty Coefficient
description: Calculates the Admiralty coefficient, displacement raised to the two-thirds power times speed cubed, divided by shaft power. It is a rough propulsive efficiency index used to compare similar ships or estimate power.
notes: Displacement in tonnes, speed in knots and power in kW follow the traditional convention; the coefficient is not dimensionless in SI. Higher values mean more speed for a given power.

name: Shaft Power from Admiralty Coefficient
description: Estimates required shaft power by rearranging the Admiralty formula: displacement to the two-thirds power times speed cubed, divided by the Admiralty coefficient Ca. It predicts power for a target speed from a known coefficient.
notes: Use the same units as when Ca was derived (tonnes, knots, kW). Accuracy depends on Ca being representative of the hull at the intended speed.

name: Wetted Surface Area (Denny-Mumford)
description: Estimates the wetted surface area of a hull using the Denny-Mumford formula, 1.7 times length times draft plus displaced volume divided by draft. Wetted area drives frictional resistance calculations.
notes: An empirical approximation for conventional hull forms; accuracy falls for unusual shapes. All lengths and volume must be in consistent metric units to give square metres.

name: Metacentric Height (GM)
description: Computes the metacentric height GM, the vertical distance from the centre of gravity up to the metacentre, as keel-to-buoyancy plus metacentric radius minus keel-to-gravity (KB + BM − KG). It is the primary measure of initial transverse stability.
notes: All heights are measured from the keel in the same units. A positive GM means the ship is stable; small or negative values indicate tenderness or capsize risk.

name: Transverse Metacentric Radius (BM)
description: Gives the transverse metacentric radius BM, the second moment of area of the waterplane divided by the displaced volume. It is the height of the metacentre above the centre of buoyancy and feeds directly into the GM calculation.
notes: I is the transverse moment of inertia of the waterplane about the centreline (units m^4); dividing by volume in m^3 yields metres. A wider waterplane sharply increases BM and stability.

name: Righting Moment (Small Angle)
description: Calculates the righting moment that restores a heeled ship to upright, as displacement mass times gravity times metacentric height times the sine of the heel angle. It quantifies the recovering torque at small angles of heel.
notes: Valid only for small heel angles where GM stays roughly constant; at larger angles the full GZ curve is needed. Heel angle is in radians and displacement is the mass, not the weight.

name: Natural Rolling Period
description: Estimates a ship's natural transverse rolling period as 2·pi times the roll radius of gyration divided by the square root of gravity times metacentric height. It is the time for one complete free roll oscillation.
notes: A larger GM gives a shorter, stiffer roll period that can feel uncomfortable. Assumes free undamped rolling in still water; the radius of gyration must reflect the loaded mass distribution.

name: Propeller Thrust (Momentum Theory)
description: Computes propeller thrust from actuator-disk momentum theory as water density times disk area times advance speed times the increase in slipstream speed (vj − va). It equals the rate of momentum imparted to the water.
notes: An idealised model ignoring blade drag, swirl and tip losses, so it overestimates real thrust. Speeds are relative to the water; vj must exceed va for positive thrust.

name: Propeller Slip Ratio
description: Gives the propeller slip ratio, one minus the advance speed divided by the theoretical pitch speed (n·p). It measures the fraction by which real advance falls short of the distance the pitch would screw through solid material.
notes: Rotational speed is in revolutions per second and pitch in metres, so n·p is the theoretical speed. Some slip is normal and necessary to generate thrust; negative slip suggests input error.

name: Propeller Thrust Coefficient
description: Computes the dimensionless thrust coefficient KT, thrust divided by water density times rotational speed squared times diameter to the fourth power. It non-dimensionalises propeller thrust for open-water performance curves.
notes: Rotational speed must be in revolutions per second (not rpm) and diameter in metres for consistency. KT is read against advance ratio J on a propeller's characteristic chart.

name: Propeller Torque Coefficient
description: Gives the dimensionless torque coefficient KQ, shaft torque divided by water density times rotational speed squared times diameter to the fifth power. It non-dimensionalises the torque a propeller absorbs.
notes: Rotational speed is in revolutions per second and diameter in metres. KQ pairs with KT and advance ratio to define open-water efficiency; the fifth-power diameter makes it very size-sensitive.

name: Propeller Open-Water Efficiency
description: Calculates open-water propeller efficiency as advance ratio J times thrust coefficient KT divided by 2·pi times torque coefficient KQ. It is the ratio of useful thrust power to shaft power in undisturbed water.
notes: All three inputs are dimensionless and must come from the same propeller operating point. The result is the propeller's efficiency alone, excluding hull and relative-rotative effects.

name: Deadweight Tonnage
description: Computes deadweight tonnage as loaded displacement minus lightship displacement. It is the total mass of cargo, fuel, stores, crew and water a ship can carry when loaded to its marks.
notes: Both displacements must be in the same tonnage units; the result is carrying capacity, not the ship's own weight. It does not equal cargo alone, since it also includes fuel and consumables.

name: Tonnes Per Centimetre Immersion (TPC)
description: Gives the tonnes needed to change a ship's mean draft by one centimetre, as waterplane area times water density divided by 100. It links added load to the resulting sinkage.
notes: Water density is in tonnes per cubic metre; the factor of 100 converts a one-centimetre layer to metres. Valid for small draft changes where the waterplane area stays roughly constant.

name: Fresh Water Allowance
description: Calculates the fresh water allowance, the increase in draft permitted when a ship moves from salt to fresh water, as displacement divided by four times TPC. The result in millimetres compensates for the reduced buoyancy of fresh water.
notes: The formula assumes standard sea water at density 1.025; it gives the extra sinkage expected in fully fresh water. Displacement and TPC must use matching tonnage units.

name: Vessel Cruising Range
description: Estimates a vessel's cruising range in nautical miles as 24 times speed times fuel onboard divided by daily fuel consumption. It converts fuel endurance in days into distance at the given speed.
notes: Speed is in knots and consumption in tonnes per day, so the factor 24 turns days into hours. Assumes constant speed and consumption with no reserve margin held back.

name: Effective (Tow-Rope) Power
description: Computes the effective or tow-rope power as total hull resistance times ship speed. It is the power that would be needed to tow the hull at that speed, before propulsive losses are added.
notes: Resistance in newtons and speed in metres per second give watts. This excludes propeller and transmission efficiency, so installed shaft power must be considerably higher.

name: Longitudinal Metacentric Radius (BML)

variables.label: Longitudinal moment of inertia of waterplane

description: Computes the longitudinal metacentric radius, BML = IL/V, the distance from the centre of buoyancy to the longitudinal metacentre, from the waterplane's longitudinal moment of inertia and the hull's displaced volume.
notes: BML governs a ship's resistance to trim (pitching); it is normally much larger than the transverse metacentric radius BM. Assumes small-angle trim and a rigid, unflooded hull.
